newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM welcomes PNG shift on mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM welcomes PNG shift on mercenaries.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday welcomed news that the government of Papua New Guinea was considering dropping plans to use foreign mercenaries against a rebellion on Bougainville island.
"There's obviously been some change, some shift in attitude and that's good," Howard told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

"It seems as though some of the mercenaries at least may be going home. If that is indicative of an overall change, then I warmly welcome that because we have always seen the use of mercenaries as a bad idea."

Australian Foreign Affairs Department chief Philip Flood flew to the troubled South Pacific nation late on Wednesday as Howard's personal envoy to discuss alternatives to the mercenary plan with PNG Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.
Australian defence intelligence chief Hugh White and Australia's former High Commissioner in Port Moresby, Allan Taylor, accompanied Flood.
Howard said he believed the PNG situation was returning to some stability and he was hopeful of a satisfactory outcome.
"It is self-evidently a bit volatile," he said. "But it does seem to me that the military leadership of Papua New Guinea is taking a very responsible attitude towards civilian disorder.
"There appears to be no attempt by the dismissed Brigadier-General (Jerry) Singirok to encourage any kind of open rebellion and that's to be applauded."
Apart from sparking PNG's current crisis, Chan's planned use of mercenaries has soured relations with neighbouring powers.
But both Australia, PNG's largest aid donor, and New Zealand backed Chan over his decision to sack Singirok after the general demanded that Chan quit over the mercenary deal.
Howard refused to give details about alternative plans but Australian media have speculated that Canberra could boost its training of PNG soldiers if Chan sent the mercenaries home.

Six of 40 foreign mercenaries left Papua New Guinea on Wednesday and told reporters in Singapore that the contract between Port Moresby and British-based Sandline International had already been terminated.
